units.text: Entrainment during Tapping of a Model Con- verter Using Two Liquid Phases
Introduction

Curtailment of carryover slag during tapping of steel from converter is of immense practical importance for quality steel production. But slag free tapping is difiicult to ensure due to the formation of draining vortex in the liquid bath.

The vortex phenomenon in regard to draining fiow from cylindrical model vessels has beenstudied by several authors using single liquid i.e in the absence of "slag" phase.1~3) Hammerschmid et al.2) concluded that presence of residual rotational motion in the vessel in conjunction with increase of angular velocity at the orifice during drainage finally causes formation of an air-core vortex which extends from the liquid surface and penetrates through the nozzle, All reported parametric effects on vortexing viz. waiting time before nozzle opening,2) eccentric placement of nozzles, 2,4,5) gas injection from vessel bottom,2,5) flow obstacles near nozzle2) etc. can be related to the above mentioned rotational motion.

The works of Sucker et al.4,5) show applicability of most of the single liquid vortex features to the two liquid case as well. Neither of these two works, however, relate to the extent of lighter phase entrainment and were restricted to detection of the vortex appearance only. Thus effectively they have disregarded the role of postformation intensification of the vortex. Also effect of another interacting vortex which forms later, though noted, was not considered in terms of entrainment.

The present model work carried out using two immiscible liquids, monitored extent of lighter phase entrainment in order to identify relative role of diverse vortex features that may influence slag entrainment in situations akin to BOF tapping. It may be worthwhile to note that true simulation of BOF tapping is not possible dueto difficulty in simulating residual rotational motion which results from decay of bath turbulence after blowing of the converter is over as also mild motion generated during vessel tilting for tapping. Nevertheless, the entrainment study such as this requires consideration of vessel shape due to its likely effect on the generation of rotational motion. This is particularly important for BOF condition where the liquid massassumes complex asymmetric shape at tapping position. were carried out using water and kerosene as the two liquids. The initial filling heights of the two liquids are indicated in the Fig. 1. The liquids were poured into the model in identical fashion in every experiments. The tap hole plug was opened after allowing the liquids to settle for a pre-decided time period. This waiting time has been shownto play a major role in the formation of vortex.

For sample collection, sample containers were placed beneath the drain hole one after the other with time gap not exceeding half a second. The volume of lighter phase in each sample was measured after allowing the sample to settle in measuring cylinder.
Thevolumepercents, thus measured, were used as index of entrainment.

Effect of Viscosity on Entrainment

Vortexing being an effect caused by generation of rotational motion in the lower liquid (heavier phase), transmission of the motion to the lighter phase is likely to influence both appearance of the vortex and build up of its intensity, Under this background, effect of viscosity of the lighter liquid on entrainment was studied. The cumulative entrainment effect of several liquids of different viscosity is shown in Fig. 4. The reduced entrainment with increased lighter phase viscosity appears to be due to increased resistance to fluid motion at the liquid-liquid interface. The effect shows feasibility of reducing slag entrainment by increasing tap slag viscosity in actual BOF situation,  Such shift of vortex origin prevented entry of lighter phase into the vortex core. It is, therefore, obvious that the primary condition for stoppage of the entrainment of the lighter liquid phase into the vortex core is partial immersion of the ball into heavier liquid. The requisite ball weight can be calculated taking into account slag layer thickness at the vessel tap position and densities of the two liquids.

The findings as above are in conformity with the work of Hammerschmid et al.2) and Dubkeand Schwerdtfeger.3) However, Suckar et al. 4) proposed altogether different mechanism.Theseauthors suggested suction of the slag cut-off ball by the vortex fiow deepinside the heavier liquid and thereby prevention of slag core vortex. Practical utilisation of this mechanism seems difficult since slight misadjustment of ball density can suck the ball still deeper and close the tap hole prematurely.
Conclusions

The cold model study with two liquids showed formation of either a single or twin vortex depending upon the extent of initial rotation of the liquids in the container. Twin vortex includes an inner core extending from air•1iquid interface to the nozzle encompassed by an outer vortex originating from the liquid-liquid interface. Lighter phase entrainment was essentially due to the outer vortex. Viscosity of the lighter phase was seen to exert considerable influence on entrainment.

Themechanism of slag arrest by floating ball technique was delineated. It was shownthat shift of vortex origin is mainly responsible for curtailment of entrainment by fioating balls partially immersedinto the heavier liquid.
